why: Strong until obliges the identification beat to arrive; a human-only flow that never identifies must stay inconclusive, not fail at the end.
Same as P2: weak until is the spec correction of 2026-09-04; strong until reintroduces the false-on-compliant-flow defect at the end of the flow.
A live human leg satisfies the opt-out obligation (spec example); dropping the clause blocks the greeting-then-agent flow.
The obligation runs from identification to opt-out, not the other way; reversed, a compliant flow fails at its opt-out input.
The first draft checked only spoken actions against calling hours; a call straight to a live agent at 6 a.m. passed. P1 is a fact about the call (corpus 39 and the evaluator test pin it).
A missing caller id must be a violation at the first action with that witness, not a hope deferred to the end of the flow.

The first draft was an always over the actions, so an open path with a perfectly good caller id was held on P4 until every branch had been observed. Caller id is set on the call request; it is known at the first action, like calling hours.
An endpoint the developer declared without an action list exists by their own account; every node it serves is declared by endpoint, never painted red.
The diff is positional: a talk declared first does not license a talk that turns up third, and the missing list must name the position the developer expected.
The denominator is the point: abandonment is measured over calls answered by a person, and a machine-answered call is neither abandoned nor in the denominator.
The rule says fifteen seconds or four rings; a fourteen-second cut-off would pass a call the rule fails.

find: if (nullFact) return { id: p.id, citation: p.citation, verdict: "inconclusive", reason: REASON_FOR_NULL[nullFact] };
replace: if (nullFact) return { id: p.id, citation: p.citation, verdict: "true", reason: REASON_FOR_NULL[nullFact] };
why: An unresolved timezone or line type must hold the call, never pass it; this is the never-guess rule of spec section 08.
Under strict policy an inconclusive verdict holds for a human; advisory is the only policy that passes it.

find:
if (verdicts.some((v) => v.verdict === "false")) return "block";
  if (verdicts.some((v) => v.verdict === "inconclusive")) return policy === "strict" ? "hold" : "pass";
replace:
if (verdicts.some((v) => v.verdict === "inconclusive")) return policy === "strict" ? "hold" : "pass";
  if (verdicts.some((v) => v.verdict === "false")) return "block";
why: A definite violation on one property outranks an undecided verdict on another: block beats hold.

find: if (!terminal) return { id: p.id, citation: p.citation, verdict: "inconclusive", reason: "the path continues through a branch that has not been observed" };
why: An open path (a branch nobody has observed) must be held, not given the end-of-flow verdict as if the object had ended.

find: return end === "true" ? { id: p.id, citation: p.citation, verdict: "true" }
replace: return end !== "true" ? { id: p.id, citation: p.citation, verdict: "true" }
why: The end-of-flow verdict turns 'no opt-out yet' into 'no opt-out ever'; inverted, the synthetic-no-optout object passes.
A talk action is synthesised speech; without the synthetic atom P2's prohibition never fires.
A stream action plays prerecorded audio, which 47 CFR 64.1200(b) treats exactly like an artificial voice.
Only the beat that speaks a declared phrase identifies; a declaration alone must not make every talk action identify.
An input whose event URL matches the declared opt-out handler offers opt-out; dropping the detection makes every synthetic flow fail P3.
Caller id presence inverted: a valid number would read as suppressed and a malformed one as present.
A five-digit string is not a dialable caller id; the lower bound is part of the validity check.
A websocket endpoint is a machine, not a person; counting it as a live leg would satisfy P2 and P3 with a bot.
Phrase matching is case-insensitive by design; a capitalised declaration must still match the spoken beat.
LTL3's third value is the whole point: an undecided prefix must not read as satisfied.
An empty negation language means the property holds on every continuation; swapping the two verdicts flips every definite answer.
The end-of-flow verdict for a terminating path decides P3; inverted, a flow with no opt-out passes and one with an opt-out fails.
An atom absent from a valuation (or null) must read false; reading it true would satisfy identifies or offers_optout by omission.
The per-state emptiness check decides which states have a non-empty omega-language; negated, the monitor's true and false verdicts are built on the wrong states.
A single node with no self edge has no infinite run through it; counting it as an accepting cycle makes a dead-end state live and an unsatisfiable obligation undecided.
A state labelled !p must refuse a letter where p is true; otherwise every negated atom in a property is ignored.
The acceptance set for an until must exclude states still owing the right-hand side; with every state accepting, F p holds on a path that never sees p.
The left branch of p U q must carry the until into the next state; without it, one p discharges the obligation forever.
p W q is q R (p | q); q R p would require !speaks on the identification beat itself, the very defect the weak-until correction removed.
Across paths a property is false if any observed path makes it false; an unobserved branch elsewhere must not downgrade a violation to a hold.
47 CFR 64.1200(c)(1) opens the window at 8am local; 7:59 must be outside.
The window closes at 9pm local; 21:00 must be outside.
Exactly 8:00 is inside the window (the rule says before 8am); an exclusive open bound would block the first minute.
Exactly 21:00 is outside the window (the rule says after 9pm, and 9:00pm itself is not before it); an inclusive close bound would allow it.
A destination with no known timezone must be three-valued (null, which the evaluator holds), never assumed inside hours.
A prefix that spans two zones which disagree at this instant is undecided; picking the first zone's answer guesses.

find: if (e.prev_hash !== prev) return { ok: false, entries: entries.length, head: prev, brokenAt: { seq: e.seq, problem: "prev_hash does not match the previous entry" } };
why: Without the link check a rewritten entry whose own hash was recomputed verifies; the chain is then a list of self-consistent entries, not a chain.

find: if (recomputed !== entry_hash) return { ok: false, entries: entries.length, head: prev, brokenAt: { seq: e.seq, problem: "entry_hash does not match the entry's canonical form" } };
why: Without recomputing each entry's hash, a rewritten body under an unchanged hash verifies.

find: if (e.seq !== expectedSeq) return { ok: false, entries: entries.length, head: prev, brokenAt: { seq: e.seq, problem: `sequence gap: expected ${expectedSeq}` } };
why: A deleted entry must surface as a sequence gap at the entry after it.
The genesis link is a published protocol constant: every persisted chain and every stranger's verifier starts from sixty-four zero nibbles.
Canonical JSON sorts keys by code point so two writers hash the same body alike; insertion order would make the hash depend on the writer.
Undefined values are omitted from the canonical form; keeping them would make the encoder throw or emit a non-JSON token.
Only safe integers are canonical; a float can print differently across runtimes and so hash differently.
